source_title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026 (So Far)?
source_excerpt:
There’s a lot for readers to love about a Kindle. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to Kindle+ (previously named Kindle Unlimited) to get unlimited access to a catalog of eligible titles or use the device to access free books via your local library . But how are you supposed to know which model to buy, given the many options available?
I’ve owned all kinds of Kindles, including the newest 2026 Kindles all the way down to a seasoned hand-me-down Kindle that predated the front light era. There are more options than ever now that the latest generation of Kindles have arrived, but you don't necessarily need to upgrade. Here's how to choose the best Kindle for you and your needs.
While you're at it, check out my other buying guides for readers, including the Best Kindle Accessories , Best E-Readers That Aren't a Kindle , Best Digital Notebooks , and Best Gifts for Book Lovers .
Updated October 2026: This guide has been updated with the new 2026 Kindle models as picks (unless the older models are on sale), plus notes on the new Kindle accessories.
If You're Interested in Older (and Cheaper) Kindles
The Best Kindle Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Julian Chokkattu Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2026, 13th Generation) $200 Amazon (16 GB, With Lock Screen Ads) $250 Amazon (32 GB, Signature Edition) The Kindle Paperwhite sports the best balance of features for most readers, including among the new generation of Kindles. For an extra $50 over the base Kindle, you'll get a warm-light option, a larger 7-inch screen, and 12 weeks of battery life. The warm light is a huge bonus if you're a nighttime reader like I am. The 2026 version of the Paperwhite is not hugely different from the 2024 edition, but you will get a slightly lighter weight and a fractionally smaller body. A couple of AI features are added—Story So Far, which you can access in your menus as “Recap” to get a spoiler-free recap of your book based on how far you've read, and a feature called Ask This Book that's still to come—but I didn't notice any major performance changes like I did between the 2024 and 2026 base Kindle. The biggest differences come with the Signature Edition, which adds an aluminum frame and two beautiful colors to choose from, plus pogo pins in the back of the device to make it compatible with the new Page Turn Cover ($80) that can add page-turn buttons onto the side of your device. It's a boon if that's a feature you're looking for, but a bummer it's only available with the more expensive model. (Both the regular 2026 Paperwhite and the 2024 Paperwhite are compatible with the cheaper Kindle Click [$35] Bluetooth page-turn remote if you want a more affordable page-turning accessory.) I love the feel of the aluminum body, but it does make it a little heavier if that's an issue for you. You'll also get an auto-adjusting front light, twice the storage, and no lock screen ads without having to pay extra. ★ Older, But Still Good: If you want a plastic model that comes in a color, shop the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite ($200) instead. It costs the same as the new model after the Amazon price hikes in August , so you might as well get the newest model if you're paying full price, but this model does have a raspberry pink version if you want a color. I also expect this model will be on sale for Black Friday, while the newer model may not be. The Cheapest Kindle Photograph: Julian Chokkattu Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle (2026, 12th Gen) $150 Amazon (Plastic, With Lock Screen Ads) $190 Amazon (Aluminum, No Ads) If you're looking to spend the least amount, there are two Kindle versions to consider: the older 2024 Kindle ($150) and the newer 2026 Kindle ($150) . While the newer one has some improvements, the older model is more likely to be on sale this holiday season. It should drop to at least $125 during sale events, though it dipped down to $104 during the most recent Prime Day. The best time to buy a Kindle is during a sale event, and if you want to stick to a budget, wait for one of these models to go on sale. But when they're not on sale and are listed at the same price, I'd get the newest model over the old. Both now cost $150 following Amazon's price hikes (the 2024 model used to cost $110), so you might as well go for the latest and greatest. Compared to the 2024 version, the 2026 Kindle has faster book-opening speeds and no lag when I exit a book. The newer model also offers a slightly warmer front light, though neither has a truly warm light like the Paperwhite or Colorsoft. I tested the more expensive aluminum-backed Kindle Aluminum, but the plastic version (which comes in the purple Ube color) is cheaper. Many features remain the same, like the 6-inch screen, 300-pixel-per-inch display, an adjustable front light, 16 GB of storage (though you can upgrade to 32 GB if you get the aluminum version), and up to six weeks of battery life. The body of the updated Kindle is a little shorter without shrinking the screen, and it weighs a bit less, going from 5.56 ounces to 4.9 ounces. The aluminum, however, is slightly heavier at 5.7 ounces. I loved the feel of it even with the extra weight, though, and the color most of all (I have the Alpine Sky blue). Both models work with the new Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth page-turner remote, but neither is compatible with the Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) , which is only compatible with 7-inch models. Ultimately, you'll save more money if you wait for a sale, and the two devices are similar enough that you won't be missing out if you choose the older model over the new. But again, if there's no sale happening, get the newest model. ★ An Aluminum Version: While the other Kindles have a Signature Edition that comes with an aluminum body and extra features, the Kindle has the Kindle Aluminum ($190) , which has the aluminum frame but not as many features. You will get 32 GB of storage (something the base Kindle has never had before) and the AI-powered Story So Far and eventually Ask This Book, but no other bonuses like an auto-adjusting front light or wireless charging. Still, it's a gorgeous, compact device; I just wish it didn't cost so much for so little. The Upgrade Pick Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Julian Chokkattu Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Colorsoft (2026, 2nd Generation) $290 Amazon (16 GB) $320 Amazon (32 GB, Signature Edition) If you already own a Kindle, a reason to consider upgrading is to get a color screen. It'll breathe life into your bookshelf with colorful covers, show your graphic novels in their true form, and let you color-coordinate your highlight system. Is it a necessity? No, especially not for adults, whose books typically don't contain color pages or pictures. You'll also get a better price on a color e-reader from Kobo, which has the Kobo Libra Colour ($260) available for cheaper and comes with page-turner buttons built in. The color isn't super vibrant on the Kindle Colorsoft (or any color e-reader) since it's an E Ink screen, and the color features only have a resolution of 150 ppi. Similar to the new Paperwhite, you'll get a 7-inch screen, 16 GB of storage, and a warm front light option, and there's a Signature Edition with an aluminum back and color frames, more storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and compatibility with the Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) . There's also compatibility with both 2026 and 2024 models for the Kindle Click ($35) page-turner remote, so you don't need to upgrade to the new Signature Edition to get a page-turning accessory. The biggest upside is that every version of the Colorsoft is also ad-free, but getting a lock-screen-ad-free Paperwhite is still cheaper than the cheapest Kindle Colorsoft. The color-body versions are available in the more expensive Signature Edition. Both models have the AI features we've seen on other Kindles, but only have eight weeks of battery life compared to the Paperwhite's 12 weeks. ★ The Older Version: You won't save any money going with the older 2024 Kindle Colorsoft ($290), at least not right now. But there's a chance it'll be on sale when this new version isn't, so keep an eye out if you want to find a Colorsoft on sale. Best for Students and Note-Takers Photograph: Nena Farrell Photograph: Nena Farrell Video: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Scribe (2nd Gen, 2024) $400 Amazon (16 GB) $400 Best Buy (16 GB) Students who want to take notes digitally but who also love to read will love a Kindle Scribe. There are now three new Kindle Scribe models, which I detail below , and my favorite is still the second-generation option from 2024, even with new generations out. It has the same 10.2-inch (300 ppi) paperlike display as the first iteration, but its white border provides a more notebook-style look. It also comes with the Premium Pen that has a soft-tipped eraser at the end. It’s easily my most-used Kindle and digital notebook because of the long battery life (up to 12 weeks) and the convenience of grabbing it for both my reading and note-taking needs. While it doesn't have as many options and layouts as a true digital notebook, the Kindle Scribe nonetheless provides enough assistance to help me organize most of the ideas jumbling around in my brain. The second-gen Scribe's software capabilities include Active Canvas, which lets you write directly in a book you’re reading, though it won’t work like true annotation. Instead, the notes appear in a small square on the screen like a Post-It note. That means it’ll always be there, and you can resize the screen to keep it less in the way. Even so, it didn’t feel ideally natural to use. It also offers Expandable Margins that let you write notes in the side panel of books, which feels a little more intuitive than Active Canvas, but still isn’t the full annotation experience you might want. There are also a couple of generative artificial intelligence features: The Refined Writing tool transforms your notes into a script font, while Summarization quickly summarizes pages of notes into bullets with a script font that you can then share from the notebook tab. Both features work well, but I never find myself reaching for them. You can download these software features onto first-generation Kindle Scribes. Notably, no device in the Scribe line was subject to the recent price increase of other Kindles.
